children: India once had a head start in semiconductors. Four decades later, it is trying to turn its design strength into an ecosystem that can actually deliver chips

India’s relationship with chips has been a story of near-misses. In 1984, the country built a fab in Mohali, three years before Taiwan’s TSMC was even founded. Then, in 1989, a fire tore through the facility just as rivals across Asia were pouring money into their own chip industries, and India’s head start quietly slipped away. What followed was three decades of consolation: India became one of the world’s best places to design a chip, but not, until now, to build one.

The vocabulary has now definitely changed. India is no longer just announcing ambition. It is confronting execution: Can factories be built and ramped? Can customers be found? Can Indian designs become products? Can equipment, materials and talent arrive alongside fabs? These were the debates at the recently concluded SEMICON India 2026, perhaps the country’s largest annual gathering of the semiconductor industry in recent years.
Onwards To Execution
The 300-mm fab is still being built at Dholera in Gujarat. Its opening remains a work in progress. Around it, a semiconductor story has begun.

India’s first phase under the India Semiconductor Mission (ISM) committed Rs 76,000 crore to foundational capabilities. By 2026, 12 semiconductor projects had been approved, representing about Rs 1.64 lakh crore of investment: one silicon fab, two compound semiconductor fabs and nine packaging facilities. Twenty-three chip tape-outs had been completed, while three units had begun production and exports.

That matters because India’s weakness was never a shortage of engineers. The country became one of the world’s major centres for chip design while remaining dependent on other countries for fabrication, advanced packaging, materials and equipment.
Now the factory floor is working to catch up with the design offices.
The Ecosystem Before Fab

Micron’s assembly and test operation is among the facilities that have entered commercial production, while Tata Electronics is pressing ahead with its Dholera fab. The Tata facility, planned as India’s first commercial 300-mm fab, has partnerships with global technology companies, including Taiwan’s Powerchip Semiconductor Manufacturing Corporation, and ASML is supporting its lithography requirements, local talent development and supply-chain resilience.
The fab is becoming an anchor around which a supply network can form.

ASML Executive Vice President Wayne Allen told BW Businessworld that the company is exploring opportunities to broaden its semiconductor supply chain capabilities and strengthen engineering capacity in India. “We are just getting started. We are learning from the broader ecosystem,” Allen said.
That ecosystem is arriving in pieces.

Lam Research has announced plans for a roughly Rs 10,000 crore silicon-component manufacturing facility in India, building on more than 25 years of engineering and R&D activity in the country. Applied Materials has announced USD 5 billion of investment through 2035, focused on research, supply-chain development and workforce expansion. Tokyo Electron plans a semiconductor training centre in Gujarat with the Japanese government to develop fab and equipment engineers.
Infineon, meanwhile, increased its India workforce by 28 per cent in a year to more than 2,800 people and expanded its technology footprint across Ahmedabad, Bengaluru and Hyderabad.

These moves indicate something the original policy debate has often obscured: a fab is not an island. It needs gases, chemicals, equipment, engineers, software, logistics and customers. It needs suppliers that can meet semiconductor-grade requirements and products designed with manufacturing in mind.
At SEMICON India, that broader ecosystem started to become visible. But, of course, that too, will take time to build up over the next four-five years and beyond.

Tata Electronics signed multiple partnerships spanning equipment, materials, packaging, design and supply chains. Its partnership with L&T Semiconductor Technologies (LTSCT) is particularly revealing: the companies will explore manufacturing LTSCT’s existing and future products through Tata’s fabrication and packaging infrastructure, connecting Indian chip design with Indian manufacturing.

LTSCT itself unveiled 40 products, including a 1,200V silicon-carbide MOSFET platform and a fully designed-in-India BLDC motor controller. Its portfolio spans power electronics, computing, connectivity and secure identity.
This is the beginning of a different kind of semiconductor story: not just factories, but products.

Japanese technology company Fujifilm agreed to invest about Rs 800 crore in a semiconductor materials manufacturing plant in Gujarat, working with Tata Electronics to localise critical raw materials and help Indian chemical manufacturers develop high-purity capabilities.
Everspin Technologies offered another glimpse of what customer creation could look like.

The US-based memory chipmaker is bringing its MRAM products to India for defence, space and electric-vehicle applications. President and CEO Sanjeev Aggarwal told BW Businessworld that the company could eventually license its technology to an Indian fab if it can build sufficient demand.
“If we can create enough demand over the next two years, then we can look at licensing our technology to an Indian fab,” Aggarwal said.
The sequence is telling: first the customer, then the manufacturing opportunity.

Everspin is also discussing packaging relationships with Indian companies, including Tata Electronics, under the OSAT model. Completed wafers could be shipped into India for packaging, assembly, testing and warehousing.
UST COO Gilroy Mathew sees another advantage in the timing. India is constructing much of its semiconductor infrastructure while artificial intelligence is reshaping chip design and manufacturing.

“India has an advantage because many other countries who have gotten the semiconductor system, they had existed before AI. So, they (advanced nations) need to unlearn a lot of things to get to the AI world…whereas in India, we are setting up the infrastructure now,” said Mathew.
UST’s joint venture with Kaynes Semicon is already operating its OSAT facility at about 60 per cent utilisation, with three customers using existing capacity.
The demand side matters just as much.

Sandisk India Vice President Subind Kumar told BW Businessworld that India’s next step should be to build a deeper IT-equipment ecosystem around laptops, servers and their components, creating domestic demand for products such as SSDs.

“Just like we did the cellphone revolution, we have to do the IT equipment revolution, where you are now going to build the whole laptop using Indian components. When you start doing it, then you build the SSD in India,” Kumar said.
That argument points to the unfinished part of India’s semiconductor strategy: factories need products, and products need markets.

Raja Manickam, Founder and CEO of iVP Semi, argues that the next phase must also reach smaller Indian companies. “It’s not a question of we don’t have the capability. But it needs time and it needs some investments,” he told BW Businessworld, referring to domestic semiconductor equipment.

The policy is moving in that direction. Semicon 2.0 (or ISM 2.0) expands support beyond fabs and packaging into equipment, materials, advanced packaging, R&D, design and talent. It carries Rs 1,27,500 crore and targets 200 chip design startups and companies and one lakh semiconductor professionals.

At Semicon India, SEMI President and CEO Ajit Manocha said the global industry had already crossed USD 1 trillion and could reach USD 2 trillion by 2030. More important for India, he said the country’s 12 first-phase projects were progressing faster than he had expected.
And his prescription for what comes next was blunt: “The ecosystem play will be the leverage for competition.”
That may be the clearest description of where India stands now.
The Hard Part Begins Now

The first fab still has to open. Packaging capacity has to ramp. Customers have to qualify Indian facilities. Suppliers have to meet semiconductor-grade standards. Indian chip companies have to move from tape-outs to recurring products. And India has to prove its manufacturing base can compete beyond government incentives.

But the story has changed. India has moved in terms of policy, started building the factories, attracting the equipment makers, developing the suppliers, recruiting the engineers and, increasingly, finding the customers.
The next chapter will be measured in wafers, packages, products and repeat orders along with investments and MoUs.
